title: Korean Power Equipment Makers' U.S. Order Backlog Hits $31B on AI Data Center Grid Demand
content:
Korea Supply Chain Brief · September 28, 2026

Three listed Korean power-equipment makers — HD Hyundai Electric, Hyosung Heavy Industries and LS Electric — are sitting on a combined order backlog of KRW 43 trillion, up more than sevenfold from KRW 5.7 trillion at the end of 2021, as U.S. grid bottlenecks from AI data center growth push buyers toward Korean transformer and switchgear makers. Here is where each company's U.S. manufacturing stands, and why aging American transmission equipment is the specific opening driving this.

Why U.S. buyers are short on power equipment

Citing TrendForce, the report says global data center power demand will reach 161 GW this year, up 31% from last year, and is projected to grow more than 30% again next year. AI servers' share of that demand is rising from 25% last year to about 33% this year and a projected 40% next year. The gap between data center demand and grid supply capacity is expected to widen sharply after 2028.

The U.S. compounds this with an aging-grid problem: domestic production of large transformers (10,000 kVA and above) has not kept pace, and import dependence has risen sharply since 2022 to more than 90% of U.S. supply today, according to the report, which cites the U.S. Department of Energy on delivery times exceeding two years for major power equipment and some transformer prices rising 4 to 9 times over the past five years. Washington's push to remove China from the grid supply chain, framing it as a national security issue, is adding to the imbalance the report describes.

Company by company: U.S. manufacturing footprint

HD Hyundai Electric

HD Hyundai Electric built the first Korean-owned local transformer plant in the U.S., opening its North American subsidiary in Montgomery, Alabama in 2011. The report describes it as the largest power transformer production facility in the area. In the U.S. market for ultra-high-voltage transformers rated 100 MVA and above, the company held a 17.2% share in 2024 and 25.7% in 2025, ranking first for two straight years, per the report. It is building a second plant on 29,000 square meters of its Alabama site for about KRW 385 billion, due to complete in April next year; the report says it will raise the Alabama plant's ultra-high-voltage transformer capacity by 50% and add capability to produce 765 kV-class products.

Hyosung Heavy Industries

Hyosung Heavy Industries centers its U.S. production on a plant in Memphis, Tennessee, acquired from Mitsubishi (Japan) in 2020. The report describes it as the only U.S. facility capable of designing and manufacturing 765 kV-class ultra-high-voltage transformers. The company is targeting more than 50% additional ultra-high-voltage transformer capacity by 2028, with the report estimating that once the expanded capacity is fully running in 2029, the Memphis plant alone could generate more than KRW 850 billion in annual local revenue. Separately, Hyosung formed a joint venture with U.S. power infrastructure firm Quanta Services in July to build what the report calls the first Korean-owned ultra-high-voltage circuit breaker production base in the U.S.; from October, the venture will produce 72.5–800 kV gas circuit breakers (GCBs) — equipment that rapidly interrupts current to prevent equipment damage during grid faults — at Quanta's Canonsburg, Pennsylvania plant. Hyosung's North American revenue topped KRW 1 trillion for the first time last year, and in February the company signed a KRW 787 billion supply deal with a major U.S. transmission operator for 765 kV transformers and reactors, which the report describes as the largest single-project contract by any Korean company operating in the U.S.

LS Electric

LS Electric is taking a different angle from its two peers, building share in local distribution equipment rather than concentrating on ultra-high-voltage transformers. The report notes that switchgear has become a focal point as AI data centers ramp up operations, since it handles power distribution and circuit protection. LS Electric acquired a switchgear manufacturer in Cedar City, Utah in 2022 (now LS Electric Utah) and completed a Bastrop, Texas campus last year covering production, R&D and design for distribution equipment.

Reading the backlog number

The combined order backlog of the three companies rose from KRW 5.7 trillion at the end of 2021 to KRW 43 trillion in the first half of this year, an increase the report attributes to the AI-driven power equipment boom. Their combined operating margin also rose to 15.5% in the first half, which the report frames as a sign that the more profitable U.S. orders are increasingly showing up in results, not just backlog.

Quick FAQ

Why are Korean power equipment makers winning U.S. orders?
U.S. domestic transformer production has not kept up with rising import dependence (over 90%) and aging grid infrastructure, while AI data centers are pushing power demand up more than 30% a year, according to TrendForce data cited in the report.

Which Korean company leads in U.S. ultra-high-voltage transformers?
HD Hyundai Electric reported a 25.7% share of the U.S. 100 MVA-plus transformer market in 2025, the top ranking for a second consecutive year, per the report.

What is different about LS Electric's U.S. strategy?
It is focused on distribution switchgear rather than the ultra-high-voltage transformers its peers emphasize.
